summary:
Ondo State stands under Nigeria's national framework. Same-sex conduct has been illegal across the country since 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex union with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The Act's reach extends beyond the couple: the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory reported in August 2026 warns that participants and guests at same-sex weddings also face prosecution.

The death-penalty layer does not reach Ondo. The twelve states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where male sodomy can be punished by death, sit in the northern part of the country. Ondo, a southern state, falls under the secular Criminal Code, where Section 217 makes it a felony for any male to commit or procure an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or private, punishable by three years' imprisonment. The offence is not defined in the Code itself; Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, a senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo State, noted the gap in a January 2017 book chapter.

Visitors should expect exposure well outside sexual conduct. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 records countrywide patterns of arrest, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people under the national framework, and the UK travel advisory of August 2026 warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the risk of death by stoning under Shari'a provisions applies only in the northern states.

Nigeria offers no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection and no recognition of same-sex relationships. Cross-dressing in public has been the subject of proposals to criminalise it, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria have been killed while official processes ran their course without charge. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found on a highway in the capital; police opened what they described as a thorough and discreet investigation, and six months later no suspects had been charged. Press coverage of Bobrisky's imprisonment in 2024 openly asked which prison the authorities would hold a crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to officials' discretion; an October 2024 panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison as a first-time offender violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.

Dating apps are a documented vector for entrapment. Kito gangs lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. Police stops produce extortion: in March 2025 a 24-year-old man was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt in the country's largest city and released after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay. The SSMPA is described by those affected as a weaponised law that produces hostility independent of its text.
tangentialFactors:
Ondo's legal position is not an outlier. The national framework, including the gross-indecency offence applicable in southern states such as Ondo, shows no documented state-specific divergence, and no protective statute at state level is recorded. Ondo is a data point within a national pattern of criminalisation, not a separate regime.

The penalty gradient across the country is steep. The maximum penalty in the northern Shari'a states can reach death by stoning, while the southern portion of the country operates under a secular code where the gross-indecency felony carries three years and the SSMPA carries up to 14 years; the overview used here records a life sentence as the southern maximum in some circumstances.

Enforcement turbulence is concentrated in the north but not confined to it. Mass arrests of LGBTQ+ Nigerians are reported as especially common in northern states, while mob violence, arbitrary detention and police extortion occur countrywide, including in southern cities such as Lagos.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office advisory of August 2026 consolidates these risks for travellers: arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty exposure under Shari'a law in northern states.

Criminalisation in Nigeria predates independence and was reinforced rather than narrowed by the 2014 statute, which consolidated colonial-era offences into a wider prohibition reaching cohabitation, public displays of same-sex relationships and the operation of gay organisations.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ondo State face two overlapping criminal exposures: Section 217 of the Criminal Code, a felony carrying three years for any male committing or procuring an act of gross indecency with another male in public or private, and the SSMPA, which carries up to 14 years and reaches cohabitation, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship, and participation in or attendance at same-sex weddings.

The undefined scope of gross indecency is a live concern in Ondo itself. Victor Oluwasina Ayeni of Adekunle Ajasin University observed in a January 2017 book chapter that the Criminal Code fails to define what constitutes an act of gross indecency, leaving the charge open to prosecutorial and police interpretation.

Residents have no statutory recourse against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex relationships carry no legal recognition. Police use of the SSMPA to justify torture and arbitrary arrests is documented nationally, and extortion at stops is reported as routine.

Correctional placement for trans detainees is decided case by case rather than by rule. Press coverage at Bobrisky's sentencing in April 2024 asked openly which prison would hold a crossdresser, and an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted is unresolved. Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians feared such proposals; no source here confirms their status, and the national statute does not explicitly criminalise trans identity.

Ondo-specific enforcement data is not sourced. The available sources record no state-level divergence from the national framework and no state protective statute, but they provide no figures on arrests, prosecutions or police practice within Ondo itself.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of trans visitors, including document and gender-marker rules, airport screening that could result in outing, and access to gender-affirming care or gendered facilities, are not addressed by any source in this inventory.

Charges and outcomes after the August 2024 killing of Abuja Area Mama remain unresolved in these sources: a police investigation was opened, and six months later no suspects had been charged. The status of the case beyond February 2025 is not recorded.

One claim rests on a public rights overview rather than a primary legal text: the 1916 date for nationwide criminalisation, the 30 May 2013 and January 2014 legislative dates, and the life-sentence figure for the south come from that overview and are not corroborated here by statute or judgment.
